plan.contextChunk: This figure shows three U-tube manometer configurations that together cover every possible relationship between gas pressure and atmospheric pressure, each labeled with the corresponding pressure equation below. The left panel depicts a closed-end manometer whose sealed arm contains a vacuum, making the height difference h the sole determinant of pressure so that P_gas = hρg. The middle panel shows an open-end manometer in which the gas-side liquid stands higher than the open (atmospheric) side, indicating the gas is below atmospheric pressure and P_gas = P_atm − hρg. The right panel reverses that situation — the open-arm liquid is higher — indicating the gas exceeds atmospheric pressure so that P_gas = P_atm + hρg. This figure introduces the manometer as a practical pressure-measuring instrument and establishes the three distinct cases that determine which formula relates the liquid-column height h to the unknown gas pressure.

interactionPlan.concept: A manometer converts an unknown gas pressure into a measurable liquid-column height h, and the correct formula (P_gas = hρg, P_atm − hρg, or P_atm + hρg) is fixed entirely by which arm is sealed/open and which side the liquid is pushed higher.
elements: three U-tube manometer panels arranged left-to-right
left panel: round gas bulb labeled 'Gas' with a stopcock valve, connected to a U-tube whose right arm is sealed ('Closed end') and contains a 'Vacuum' above the mercury
left panel: gray mercury column higher in the closed arm, double-headed vertical arrow labeled 'h' spanning the two menisci
left panel: formula below reading P_gas = hρg
middle panel: gas bulb + stopcock, U-tube with right arm 'Open end' topped by a downward arrow labeled 'P_atm'
middle panel: mercury higher on the gas (left) side than the open side, double-headed arrow 'h' between menisci
middle panel: formula below reading P_gas = P_atm − hρg
right panel: gas bulb + stopcock, U-tube with right arm 'Open end' and downward 'P_atm' arrow
right panel: mercury higher on the open (right) side than the gas side, double-headed arrow 'h' between menisci
right panel: formula below reading P_gas = P_atm + hρg
light-purple fill for gas bulb and gas-side tube above the mercury
gray fill for the mercury (liquid) in all U-tubes

interactions.label: Manometer configuration
interactions.teaches: The physical situation — sealed vacuum arm, gas pushing the liquid up, or atmosphere pushing the liquid up — selects which of the three pressure formulas applies; the formula is a consequence of the geometry, not a free choice

interactions.label: Gas pressure P_gas (mmHg)
interactions.teaches: For the active configuration the column height h tracks P_gas in real time: in the closed-end tube h equals P_gas directly, while in the open-end tubes h equals the gap between P_gas and P_atm, so h shrinks to zero as P_gas approaches atmospheric pressure

Clicking the h arrow walks through the hydrostatic-balance derivation for that tube: pressures at the same horizontal level in a connected liquid are equal, so equating the gas-side and reference-side pressures at the lower meniscus yields the panel's formula and reveals why the sign of hρg flips between the two open-end cases

demo_steps.title: Closed-end: vacuum reference
demo_steps.narration: With the right arm sealed and evacuated, the only force on the closed-arm meniscus is the gas pressure, so the height h alone balances it: P_gas = hρg. Drag the slider and watch h grow in direct proportion to P_gas.

demo_steps.title: Open-end, gas below atmosphere
demo_steps.narration: Now the open arm feels P_atm. The gas side stands higher, meaning the atmosphere is winning, so P_gas = P_atm − hρg. As you raise P_gas toward 760 mmHg the height difference h collapses to zero.

demo_steps.title: Open-end, gas above atmosphere
demo_steps.narration: Push P_gas above 760 mmHg and the open-arm liquid is driven higher instead: the gas is winning, so P_gas = P_atm + hρg. The same instrument reads both sub- and super-atmospheric pressures; only the sign in front of hρg changes.

demo_steps.title: Derive the formula
demo_steps.narration: Click the h arrow in any panel to step through the equal-pressure-at-equal-depth argument. You will see that all three formulas are the same hydrostatic balance evaluated against a different reference pressure (vacuum = 0, or P_atm on the higher or lower side).

interactionPlan.keyInsight: All three manometer equations are one hydrostatic-balance rule — equal pressure at equal depth in a connected liquid — and the only thing that changes between them is the reference pressure (vacuum vs. atmosphere) and which side it acts on, which fixes the sign of the hρg term.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Lay out three U-tube panels in a horizontal row with generous spacing. Gas bulbs as light-purple circles on the upper left of each tube with a small stopcock symbol; mercury as a medium-gray fill occupying the U-bend and rising to different levels in the two arms. Left panel: cap the right arm with a rounded 'Closed end' and label the empty space above its mercury 'Vacuum'; middle and right panels: leave the right arm open with a short downward black arrow labeled 'P_atm' above it. Draw the height difference as a thin double-headed vertical arrow labeled 'h' with horizontal tick lines at each meniscus. Below each panel render the matching formula in italic serif math (P_gas = hρg; P_gas = P_atm − hρg; P_gas = P_atm + hρg). When the toggle or slider changes, animate the mercury levels smoothly and keep only the active panel's formula visually emphasized (e.g. bold/dark) while the others dim, so the learner connects geometry to equation. Use consistent colors across panels: purple gas, gray mercury, black labels and arrows.

authoredContext:
A manometer is a device similar to a barometer that can be used to measure the pressure of a gas trapped in a container. A closed-end manometer is a U-shaped tube with one closed arm, one arm that connects to the gas to be measured, and a nonvolatile liquid (usually mercury) in between. As with a barometer, the distance between the liquid levels in the two arms of the tube ( h in the diagram) is proportional to the pressure of the gas in the container. An open-end manometer ( ) is the same as a closed-end manometer, but one of its arms is open to the atmosphere. In this case, the distance between the liquid levels corresponds to the difference in pressure between the gas in the container and the atmosphere.

A manometer can be used to measure the pressure of a gas. The (difference in) height between the liquid levels ( h ) is a measure of the pressure. Mercury is usually used because of its large density.

Three diagrams of manometers are shown. Each manometer consists of a spherical pink container filled with gas on the left that is connected to a U-shaped, sealed tube by a valve on its right. The top of the U aligns with the gas-filled sphere and the U, which extends below, contains mercury. The first manometer has a sealed tube. The sealed end to the upper right in the diagram is labeled “closed end” and “vacuum.” The mercury level is higher in the right side of the tube than in the left. The difference in height is labeled “h.” Beneath this manometer illustration appears the label P subscript gas equal sign h rho g. The second manometer has an open-ended tube, which is labeled “open end.” At this opening in the upper right of the diagram is the label P subscript atm. The mercury level is higher in the left side of the tube than in the right. This difference in height is labeled “h.” Beneath this manometer illustration appears the label P subscript gas equal sign P subscript atm minus sign h rho g. The third manometer has an open-ended tube and is similar to the second manometer except that the mercury level is higher in the right side of the tube than in the left. This difference in height is labeled “h.” Beneath this manometer illustration appears the label P subscript gas equal sign P subscript a t m plus h rho g.
